_comment: Whole concepts Cambridge 0097 requires at Stage 5 that the source pack never contained. Authored from the supplied Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 5 and Learner's Book 5, in the voice the units already use. Each EXTENDS the subject of the unit it joins: the plant units gain non-flowering plants and adaptation to climate, and the states-of-matter unit gains the named common gases, the atmosphere, and pollution. The objectives that would need a NEW unit - sound, forces, magnetism, diet and digestion, predator and prey - are recorded in _needsNewUnit rather than force-fitted.
_vehicle: concepts, appended to the unit's own array and rendered by the shell as 'The lesson'. Appended and never inserted, because the shell renders in array order. Safe on a live course: complete('lesson') fires on a button press, not on a count of concepts, and complete() is add-only.
source: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 5 and Learner's Book 5 (Cambridge University Press), authored 2026-09-17.
_minimumCovered: Objectives closed by these concepts. Coverage is a number that only goes up.

_needsNewUnit._comment: No Grade 5 unit covers these subjects at all. The grade has six units, one per content sub-strand of the 2018 framework it was built to - Plants twice, States of matter, Light twice, The Earth and beyond - and none of them is a home for any of the following.
_needsNewUnit.5Ps.01, 5Ps.02, 5Ps.03: Sound: made by vibrating sources, described by pitch and volume, and how to change them. A sound unit. Stage 5's Ps sub-strand in 0097 IS sound, and the two units this grade spends on light are where 0846 put its Ps.
_needsNewUnit.5Pf.01, 5Pf.02, 5Pf.03: Forces: naming a range of them, multiple forces on an object at rest, and force diagrams. A forces unit. Grade 6 Unit 4 carries the Stage 6 forces objectives and cannot also carry Stage 5's.
_needsNewUnit.5Pe.01, 5Pe.02, 5Pe.03: Magnets, magnetic materials, forces acting at a distance and different magnetic strengths. A magnetism unit; the word `magnet` appears nowhere in Grade 5.
_needsNewUnit.5Bp.01, 5Bs.04: An adequate balanced diet, and the human digestive system. A human-biology unit. Grade 6 Unit 1 teaches digestion under the old framework's placement; diet is taught nowhere, and Grade 5's only `nutrient` text is about minerals in soil for plants.
_needsNewUnit.5Be.03: The common adaptations of predator and prey animals. 5Be.01 is closed below on plants, where this grade has units; predator and prey needs animals, and Grade 5 teaches none.

concepts.title: Plants That Never Flower
concepts.explanation:
Everything in this unit so far has begun with a seed, and every seed you have looked at came from a flower. That is true of most of the plants around you - and it is not true of all of them, which is worth knowing before you decide that flowers are simply what plants do.

Some plants never produce a flower at all, and so never produce a seed. Look at a damp wall or the shady side of a rock and you may find moss: a low green cushion with no flower on it, ever. Look at a shaded stream bank for a fern, with its tall divided leaves curled at the tip when young. Turn a fern leaf over in the right season and you find rows of small brown dots on the underside. Those are not seeds. They are cases holding spores, and a spore is far smaller and far simpler than a seed - a single cell in a tough coat, with no food store packed around it and no baby plant already formed inside.

So these plants reproduce, but by a different route. The spores are shed in enormous numbers and carried on the air. Most land somewhere useless and die; a few land somewhere damp and grow. That is why ferns and mosses are found in wet and shady places and almost never in dry open ones: a spore has no food store to live on while it establishes itself, so it needs water immediately.

Conifers are a third case and an in-between one. A pine or a cypress makes seeds, so it is not like a moss, but it produces them in cones rather than in flowers. The seeds sit naked on the scales of the cone instead of being wrapped in a fruit.

The useful way to hold all this is as three groups rather than one rule: plants that flower and make seeds inside fruits, plants that make seeds in cones without flowers, and plants that make no seeds at all and use spores.
concepts.example: A gardener wanting more of a hibiscus collects its seeds from the dried fruit. A gardener wanting more of a fern cannot - there are no seeds to collect. They divide the root clump instead, or let the spores from the leaf undersides find their own damp corner.

concepts.title: Built for the Place They Live
concepts.explanation:
A flower's bright petals are not decoration; they are there to bring an insect in. That is a useful idea with a name, and the name reaches much further than flowers: an adaptation is a feature of a living thing that suits it to the place it lives. Adaptations are not decisions. No plant chose its leaves. Over very long times, the individuals whose features happened to suit the place survived and left more offspring, and those features became common.

Once you look for them, the place a plant lives is written all over it.

A plant in a HOT DRY place has to hold on to water. A cactus has no broad leaves at all - they are reduced to spines, which lose almost no water and keep animals off besides - and it stores water in a thick fleshy stem with a waxy skin. An acacia has tiny leaves for the same reason, drops them altogether in the worst of the dry season, and sends roots down many metres to reach water no shallow-rooted plant can touch.

A plant in a WET place has the opposite problem: too much water and not enough light under the canopy. So it grows broad thin leaves to catch what light there is, and many have a pointed tip that sheds rain rather than letting it sit and rot the leaf.

A plant in a COLD place grows low and close to the ground, out of the wind, often in a dense cushion that holds a pocket of warmer air around itself.

Animals show the same logic. A camel stores fat in its hump and can go days without drinking. A desert fox has enormous ears that radiate heat away; an arctic fox has small ones that hold it in - the same organ, adapted in opposite directions by opposite problems.

The test of whether you have understood an adaptation is whether you can say what problem it solves. Spines instead of leaves is not just an odd feature of cacti; it is an answer to the question of how to photosynthesise without drying out.
concepts.example: Two trees grow a hundred metres apart, one on a dry ridge and one beside a stream. The ridge tree has small thick leaves and a deep root; the stream tree has broad thin ones and roots near the surface. Neither is a better tree. Each is built for its own few metres of ground.

concepts.title: The Gases Around Us
concepts.explanation:
You have used the particle model for solids, liquids and gases, and you have watched water turn into a gas and back. Now the gases themselves deserve naming, because "gas" is not one substance any more than "metal" is.

Five are worth knowing at this stage, and all five are gases at ordinary room temperature. NITROGEN is the one there is most of, and it is unreactive - it mostly just sits there, which is exactly why it is useful for keeping packaged food from spoiling. OXYGEN is the one you and every animal need, and the one a fire needs; nothing burns without it. CARBON DIOXIDE is what you breathe out and what a plant takes in to make its food. WATER VAPOUR is water as a gas, and it is invisible - the white cloud above a kettle is not water vapour but tiny droplets of liquid that have cooled back out of it. HYDROGEN is the lightest of all gases, so light that a balloon filled with it pulls upwards.

All of these are invisible, which is worth saying plainly, because it is the reason people doubt gases are real matter at all. Invisibility is not a rule about gases, though - it is just true of these particular ones. Bromine gas is orange-brown and you can watch it fill a jar.

The air around you is not a single gas but a mixture of several, and that mixture has a name: the ATMOSPHERE, a layer of air wrapped around the whole Earth. It is mostly nitrogen, with a smaller amount of oxygen, a very small amount of carbon dioxide, and varying water vapour. Go high enough - up a mountain, or in an aeroplane - and there is less of it in each breath, which is why climbers tire so quickly and why high aircraft are sealed and pumped.

The atmosphere is thin compared with the planet it wraps. If the Earth were the size of an orange, the air worth breathing would be thinner than the peel.
concepts.example: A jar is held upside down and pushed into a bowl of water, and the water will not rise into it. Something is already in there holding the water out, and it is not nothing - it is air, a mixture of gases, taking up space exactly as a solid or liquid would.

concepts.title: When People Spoil the Air and Water
concepts.explanation:
You have seen that most of the water on Earth is not pure - it has substances dissolved in it. Some of those arrived naturally: rain picks up gases as it falls, and a river dissolves minerals from the rock it runs over. That is not pollution. POLLUTION is the adding of substances by PEOPLE in a way that harms the environment, and the distinction matters, because otherwise the word means nothing more than "not perfectly clean".

Air pollution is the easiest to see. Smoke from burning rubbish, exhaust from vehicles, dust and fumes from a factory chimney - all of it puts substances into the atmosphere that were not there before. The harm is real and often local: smoke makes asthma worse and irritates eyes, and a city sitting under still air on a windless day can be measurably harder to breathe in.

Water pollution is often harder to see and that is precisely what makes it dangerous. Waste tipped into a river, fertiliser washed off a field, or a fuel spill can leave water that looks perfectly clear. Clear is not the same as clean: the substances that matter most are dissolved, in pieces far too small to see, and no amount of looking will find them. A filter will take out the mud and leave every one of them behind.

Land can be polluted too, by waste buried or dumped, and plastic is the example everyone has seen - it does not rot away as a leaf does, so it stays where it is dropped for a very long time.

Two things are worth holding on to. The first is that pollution is a question of quantity and place: carbon dioxide is a natural part of the atmosphere and a pollutant when there is far more of it than there was. The second is that because pollution is put there by people, it can be reduced by people, which is not true of a natural process. Burning less, spraying less, and taking waste somewhere it can be dealt with are all decisions.
concepts.example: A stream runs past two villages. Above the first it is clear; below the second it is also clear, and the fish have gone. Looking cannot tell the two stretches apart, because what changed is dissolved. A clear stream is evidence about mud, and no evidence at all about pollution.
